item.title: Facing Criticism, Trump Administration Says It’s Investigating Megaspeed
item.description:
The Justice and Commerce Departments announced late Monday that they were pursuing a criminal investigation of Megaspeed, a Singapore company once led by a woman whom U.S. officials believe worked as a Chinese intelligence asset while having an affair with Nvidia’s chief executive.

The announcement appeared to be an effort to counter criticism that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was slow to investigate Megaspeed. It has become the most prominent example of companies that American authorities believe are skirting export rules on the powerful artificial intelligence chips made by Nvidia, the world’s leading manufacturer.

Nvidia exports have exposed a rift in the Trump administration between officials who believe American A.I. technology needs to be kept out of China for national security reasons and others who want a more hands-off approach to export controls.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a TV interview on Friday that his department had been pushing for months to add Megaspeed to a trade blacklist, but that the Commerce Department “holds the pen.”

“You will have to ask them about their internal processes,” he said.

That the Justice Department was included in the Monday night announcement appeared to add heft to the investigation’s importance and signaled to critics that administration officials did not intend to ignore the issue.

Megaspeed was created and led for a time by Alice Huang, who U.S. officials say was an asset for Chinese intelligence. The New York Times reported last year that she and Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, had a close relationship, and last week Mr. Huang admitted that he had been unfaithful to his wife with Ms. Huang.

Mr. Huang resigned from Nvidia last week following another revelation that he had had a relationship with a woman who worked for him. It was a stunning downfall for an executive who led a firm that for a time was the most valuable publicly traded company in the world.Megaspeed has said that it complies with all laws and that Ms. Huang currently has no role in the company. She has not returned requests for comment, and the Chinese government has dismissed the spying claims.

The Monday night news release confirming the criminal investigation was also unusual because officials do not typically discuss their inquiries until they are completed. The departments said that they would work together to “bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred.”

President Trump on Monday acknowledged that Mr. Bessent and Mr. Lutnick had been at odds over how hard to crack down on a loophole that has allowed China to access advanced A.I. chips through data centers in other countries.

“One wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blowup with China,” Mr. Trump said of his two cabinet secretaries. “Both are acceptable, but they’re different views.”

The news release said that the Commerce Department had initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations. In May 2025, the department requested records from Nvidia on its sales to Megaspeed. Commerce officials visited the company in June 2025 and interviewed Ms. Huang, it said.

The Justice Department then took the lead role in the Megaspeed criminal investigation, the news release said.

The New York Times reported last week that the Commerce Department investigation was halted last fall under atypical circumstances, after department investigators received an email from Nvidia’s general counsel seeking information about the inquiry.

Nvidia’s general counsel said that a top official at the department had given him permission to reach out about the case, alarming others in the department. The incident raised questions about what Commerce officials had discussed with Nvidia, and some viewed the interaction as potentially tainting the case. It was then transferred to the Justice Department.

The Commerce Department also said that Nvidia had placed Megaspeed on its “no-sell” list in June 2025.

But trade records obtained by The Times from ImportGenius, a data platform, show that Speedmatrix, a Megaspeed subsidiary in Malaysia, continued receiving large shipments of Nvidia technology for eight months after that.

Between October 2026 and February 2026, Speedmatrix received shipments of more than $800 million of export-controlled Nvidia A.I. technology, including Blackwell and H200 chips, which were banned from being sent to China.

Most of the Speedmatrix shipments went through third-party manufacturers that buy chips from Nvidia and make them into servers. But in February 2026, trade records show that Nvidia International Inc. sent a $13 million shipment of electronic equipment to Speedmatrix.

Nvidia provided a similar statement to The Times about the “block list” last week. It said that it received permission from the Commerce Department to ship some repair parts to Megaspeed after imposing its “block.”

Nvidia continues to list Megaspeed on its website as a cloud partner. Megaspeed advertised the relationship as recently as October, calling its Indonesian unit “a premier business partner of Nvidia.”

The Commerce Department said it had charged 17 defendants across six separate investigations over allegations of smuggling and sharply increased monetary penalties compared with those in the Biden administration.

Mr. Lutnick has clashed in recent months with other senior officials over rules that would clamp down on data centers in Southeast Asia that serve Chinese clients. The Commerce Department issued that rule Monday, but took the unusual step of saying that it had been “written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council,” both agencies it had clashed with.

item.title: As Trump and Xi Mingle, Their Governments Are Arming Up
item.description:
In front of the cameras, President Trump and China’s Xi Jinping have showcased a budding friendship, cemented by state visits, friendly pats on the arm and the occasional shared laugh.

But the public cordiality masks a different reality. Their governments are hardening their economic defenses and putting up new barriers to trade and investment. It has become more difficult for the two countries to invest, trade or do business with each other.

More good will is expected when Mr. Trump arrives in the Chinese city of Shenzhen this week for his third meeting with Mr. Xi this year. Yet the divide between their governments is becoming harder to ignore. Each meeting has been preceded by fresh economic offensives that are driving the world’s two largest economies further apart.

Shortly before Mr. Trump was scheduled to land in Asia, his administration moved to restrict China’s access to advanced artificial intelligence chips through data centers outside its borders, proposing a new rule to close a loophole that experts said would further inflame tensions. On Tuesday, China called the rule a “textbook case of economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction” that “disrupts the stability of global industrial and supply chains.”

It was the latest in a series of moves from both China and the United States in recent weeks to label new sectors of their economies off limits in the name of national security. Beijing has designated more technologies as strategically vital, placing tighter controls on their export. Washington has proposed barring American investment in Chinese biotechnology, hypersonic weapons and artificial intelligence.

The confrontation has spilled beyond their two countries’ borders into global supply chains. China is building a fortress around technologies and critical materials on which much of the world depends, forcing other countries and multinational companies to contend with the fallout.

“There are more barriers than bridges being built,” said Ben Kostrzewa, a partner at the law firm Hogan Lovells in Hong Kong. “Each of these moves on its own is another brick in the wall and it is becoming harder and harder to invest in the other country.”

The steady buildup of those barriers began nearly a decade ago as a tit-for-tat tariff war during Mr. Trump’s first term. It has evolved into a far broader showdown for economic and technological supremacy.

China, in particular, has shifted its tactics. Once largely content to answer American tariffs and sanctions with reciprocal measures that were often symbolic, Beijing is now going on the offensive. It is wielding its dominance in manufacturing and critical supply chains to remind Washington — and the rest of the world — of the costs of confronting it.

The rivalry reached a low point last year, when both sides imposed tariffs so steep they amounted to a de facto trade embargo. China then threatened to tighten its controls on rare earths, the essential materials used in everything from smartphones and electric vehicles to fighter jets.

In October 2025, Mr. Trump and Mr. Xi eased tensions by agreeing to a truce and reciprocal state visits.

The two visits this year were heavy on ceremony. When Mr. Trump traveled to Beijing in May, he was greeted by military bands and cheering children. When Mr. Xi landed in Maryland in September, he was welcomed on the tarmac by Mr. Trump. There have been raised glasses, shared walks and moments of banter.

After Mr. Xi’s visit two months ago, the two governments agreed to extend their yearlong truce and reduce tariffs on $60 billion worth of goods. Yet neither side formally confirmed the extension until hours before the agreement was set to expire, just a week before Mr. Trump’s planned arrival in China.

Even then, the reprieve was limited. The renewed truce, which suspended certain tariffs and export controls, runs only through January.

And despite Beijing’s pledge to ease restrictions on exports of rare-earth metals and other critical minerals, some American companies still struggle to obtain supplies, said Erin Browne, the U.S. Treasury Department’s under secretary for international affairs.

“We’re making sure that we’re getting equal treatment across companies, across sectors, but also across materials or rare earths,” Ms. Browne said. “The strength of the relationship between our two presidents goes a long way in helping to move that along.”

Yet the personal rapport has done little to restrain an emboldened China, which has signaled it is no longer afraid of escalating economic warfare.

Beijing has strengthened its arsenal of countermeasures against American blacklists of its companies. It has created new legal mechanisms to block foreign sanctions, and Chinese companies have brought legal actions against foreign businesses, including JPMorgan Chase and Citibank, in Chinese courts for complying with American restrictions.

This year, Beijing introduced sweeping rules empowering regulators to inspect corporate records and prevent executives from leaving China if their companies are found to be helping to shift supply chains out of the country.

It has also established a national security review system for foreign investments, using it to block Meta’s $2 billion acquisition of Manus and SoftBank’s $5.4 billion takeover of ABB Robotics.

Together, these developments reflect “a very prominent change” in China’s approach, said Zhao Minghao, a professor at Fudan University. Beijing is assembling legal and regulatory tools built around economic and technological security, he said, and “exploring using actual cases to give these laws ‘teeth,’ so that they can truly be implemented and put to use.”

Its new strategy aims to protect control over the technologies and industries that give it a competitive edge.

Beijing has recently started restricting exports of dozens of technologies related to artificial intelligence, biotechnology and solar power. Under the rules, Chinese companies need government approval before transferring or sharing the covered technologies overseas.

For its part, Washington is seeking to cut off the capital that helps finance China’s technological ambitions. A Treasury Department proposal to expand those investment limits could make investing in broad swaths of China’s technology sector nearly impossible.

“We’re in the early stages of financial decoupling,” said H.K. Park, managing director and national security expert at Crumpton Global.

Analysts in both countries see little prospect of reversing the ever-wider restrictions on trade, technology and capital.

That leaves Mr. Xi and Mr. Trump with a shrinking set of issues on which they can strike deals. When the two leaders meet in Shenzhen, they may find room to bargain over tariffs. But the technologies, investments and critical materials at the heart of their rivalry are becoming harder to negotiate.

“Tariffs are a minor issue,” said Zhou Yong, a partner at the JunHe Law Offices in Beijing. They are among the few areas where both governments can still reach agreement.

“The real sticking points are competition in A.I., high tech, and chips, and China’s export curbs on rare earths,” he said.

“These are higher-stakes bargaining chips that both sides feel difficult to negotiate now.”

item.title: Disney Plans to Finance Growth With $3 Billion in Cost Savings
item.description:
Disney’s long-dead stock price has climbed 19 percent since Josh D’Amaro took over as chief executive in March. On Tuesday, he gave Wall Street a glimpse of how he plans to keep it going.

To drive growth, Disney said it would cut $3 billion in annual operating costs by 2029, with most of the savings earmarked for reinvestment in its businesses. Spending on content will increase 9 percent in the coming year, for instance, to $26 billion. The marketing budget for streaming will also rise. Disney also said it would triple its original programming in overseas markets over the next three years, citing the importance of locally produced content in attracting and engaging Disney+ subscribers.

Upgrading technology and expanding the use of artificial intelligence are also priorities. Disney announced, for instance, that it had started testing an A.I. tool — developed with Google — to simplify planning and booking vacations at Walt Disney World. Disney+ will add podcasts and more live sports. Videos from TikTok creators will arrive on the service next month.

How will Disney achieve the savings? The company didn’t say. But deep job cuts are expected early next year.

Mr. D’Amaro made the announcements as part of an upbeat fourth-quarter earnings report. In a surprise, however, Disney said it would stop disclosing operating profit for its entertainment streaming business. Netflix, Disney and Warner Bros. Discovery all stopped reporting subscriber totals in recent years. But most of Disney’s biggest rivals, including Netflix, NBCUniversal and Paramount Skydance, continue to provide detailed financial information about streaming profitability.

Disney is making the change after reaching a double-digit annual profit margin for streaming, a yearslong goal. The margin was nearly 12 percent.

Disney justified the decision by saying it was focused on the financial performance of its entertainment division as a whole — how much income it generates from its movies and television shows across streaming, traditional television, the box office, third-party licensing and consumer products. (A less charitable reading: Disney is reducing scrutiny of streaming margins just as increased spending could put pressure on them.)

For the quarter that ended on Oct. 3, Disney had revenue of $25.95 billion, a 16 percent increase compared with a year earlier. Adjusted per-share profit increased 59 percent, to $1.77. Both results beat analyst expectations.

Disney benefited from an extra week in its fiscal calendar; improved streaming profitability; a bump in merchandise licensing revenue ahead of “Avengers: Doomsday,” which arrives next month; and strong ticket sales for “Toy Story 5.” ESPN was bolstered by strong advertising sales and Disney’s acquisition of the NFL Network. Disney’s theme park and cruise businesses delivered $1.6 billion in operating profit, a 23 percent increase compared with a year earlier.

Disney also said it would increase its annual dividend by 33 percent, to $2 a share, and spend another $9 billion on stock buybacks in the coming year.

item.title: Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia
item.description:
The Trump administration’s proposal to restrict China’s access to advanced A.I. chips overseas rattled Southeast Asia on Tuesday, threatening a data center investment boom fueled by Chinese companies using the region to sidestep U.S. restrictions on Nvidia’s most powerful chips.

Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Singapore have become offshore computing hubs for Chinese companies such as Alibaba and ByteDance. Data center operators in those countries provide the Chinese firms with remote access to advanced Nvidia chips they cannot buy directly or bring into China.

The strategy has drawn billions of dollars in investment to the region. But in Washington, officials seeking tighter controls on China’s A.I. sector have increasingly viewed data centers as a workaround that poses economic and national security risks.

Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was ousted last week after revelations he had an affair with a woman who formed a Singaporean data center company called Megaspeed. U.S. authorities deemed the woman, Alice Huang, to be an asset for Chinese intelligence services, and they are investigating Megaspeed over allegations of smuggling chips to China. China has denied that Ms. Huang was spying for it.

Separately, Nvidia’s board of directors announced on Tuesday that it had established a committee to oversee “the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.” Nvidia’s board is engaged in a search for a permanent successor to Mr. Huang. The company’s interim chief executive, Colette Kress, is set to preside over the release of the company’s latest quarterly financial results later on Tuesday.

Shares of technology companies tumbled on Tuesday. In trading in Hong Kong, Alibaba fell 5 percent, while Tencent’s stock dropped nearly 4 percent. The Chinese A.I. firms MiniMax Group fell 7 percent and Z.AI Co. declined 5 percent. In the United States, tech stocks mostly stabilized from a sell-off that day before. Nvidia shares were up slightly ahead of the start of regular trading in New York.

Governments across Southeast Asia were scrambling to assess the administration’s 132-page policy, released by the Commerce Department on Monday, as President Trump traveled to Asia for diplomatic meetings.

The timing illustrated how A.I. has moved to the center of global diplomacy. Mr. Trump was expected to meet leaders of several affected countries at the ASEAN summit of 11 Southeast Asian nations in Manila. Then, he traveled to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation, or APEC, forum.

The rules, which take effect in 90 days, will require overseas data center operators to obtain a license from the United States government before supplying a “significant volume” of computing power to companies based in countries deemed high-risk, including China, Iran and Russia.

Licenses would also be required to export advanced chips to companies headquartered in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia or Brazil, countries the Trump administration identified as posing a heightened smuggling risk.

The Singaporean government said in a statement on Tuesday that it was investigating Megaspeed and was “engaging the relevant U.S. authorities on the scope and implementation of the measure.”

“As a global hub for technology and trade, Singapore will continue to safeguard the integrity of our business environment and continued access to advanced semiconductors and computing capabilities for legitimate companies operating here, and act against those who flout our laws,” the statement read.

Indonesia said it was seeking industry input and pledged to enforce American export controls. The government is developing a trade framework to “facilitate legitimate trade” while preventing sensitive technologies from being “diverted or misused,” the country’s Government Communication Agency said.

Steve Okun, chief executive of APAC Advisors, a geopolitical consulting firm, said countries such as Malaysia had benefited from maintaining close ties with Washington and Beijing. The new restrictions could make that balancing act harder to sustain.

“The ‘don’t make us choose’ era is coming to an end,” he said. “When it comes to A.I. and sensitive technologies, countries will need to choose the U.S.-led tech stack versus China.”

Ong Kian Ming, Malaysia’s former deputy minister for investment, trade and industry, said he hoped the Trump administration, which has been divided over A.I. chip export restrictions, would revise the rules before they take effect.

Otherwise, he said, the restrictions could create an opening for Chinese companies to offer competing chips. “This may mitigate some of the negative impact of not allowing these players to access Nvidia GPU chips,” he said.

Xinyun Wu contributed reporting.

item.title: Fed Governor Cook Won’t Attend White House Hearing Without Changes
item.description:
Lisa D. Cook, the Federal Reserve governor that President Trump is trying to fire, will not attend a White House hearing to discuss allegations that she committed mortgage fraud without major changes to a process that her lawyers have called a “façade.”

In a letter to the White Housed on Nov. 16, a lawyer for Ms. Cook reiterated his opposition to the Trump administration’s investigation, which he said was predetermined to find the Fed governor guilty. Ms. Cook has not been charged with any wrongdoing.

“Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution’s unique status and independence,” wrote Abbe David Lowell, who represents Ms. Cook.

The Federal Reserve Act stipulates that a president is only allowed to remove a governor if there is “cause” to do so. That has typically meant malfeasance or a dereliction of duty. Mr. Lowell accused the White House of convening the hearing to “manufacture” that cause.

“Consequently, this committee process appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook or to unreasonably manufacture a supposed ‘adverse inference’ if she does not participate in a process that does not comport with the requirements of a fair hearing.”

The main issue that Ms. Cook’s legal team has had with the hearing, which was initially scheduled for Nov. 5 and pushed to December, is that it is stacked with Mr. Trump’s political appointees, some of whom have already publicly said that the Fed governor should be fired.

The committee includes Kevin Hassett, the director of the National Economic Council; Keith Sonderling, the Labor secretary, who is serving as acting director of a government ethics office; and Andrea Lucas, the chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.

Mr. Hassett, for example, has accused Fed officials of acting in a partisan manner. He has also defended Mr. Trump’s ability to fire Ms. Cook and called for her to take a leave of absence when the allegations were first raised.

In his letter on Monday, Mr. Lowell said that “Mr. Hassett’s continued presence on the committee remains unacceptable.”

Ms. Cook’s lawyers have also taken issue with the fact that the White House has not shared documents containing evidence that it says it will present at the hearing, while demanding that the Fed governor immediately turn over any relevant information.

“You have not explained why that asymmetry comports with basic standards of practice and fairness,” Mr. Lowell wrote. “Although Governor Cook is open to providing documents and information in her possession, she has no obligation to do so while the committee hides the material that it purports to already have gathered.”

The hearing is a central part of Mr. Trump’s renewed attempt to remove Ms. Cook after the Supreme Court in June ruled against the administration and said the Fed governor was not given sufficient due process.

Mr. Trump has long sought more control over the central bank, which has refused to accede to his demands for lower borrowing costs. Ms. Cook has not been the only target. Last year, the administration went after Jerome H. Powell, who stepped down as Fed chair in May, for his handling of costly renovations of the central bank’s headquarters. Mr. Trump faced a number of legal setbacks and in September, the Fed’s independent internal watchdog found no evidence of wrongdoing on Mr. Powell’s part.

Mr. Powell decided to stay on at the Fed as a governor even after Mr. Trump’s pick to replace him, Kevin M. Warsh, took over the top job. Mr. Powell’s term officially ends in January 2028.

Appointments to the Board of Governors must be confirmed by the Senate, which will in January be controlled by Democrats after a bruising midterms defeat for Republicans. The Senate Banking Committee, which manages the nominations process, is likely to block any of Mr. Trump’s nominees, suggesting that if there are vacancies, the president will not have the capacity to install loyalists into those positions.

Still, Mr. Trump has yet to waver on his efforts to oust Ms. Cook. Since August, Ms. Cook’s lawyers and the administration have been in regular contact, according to correspondence viewed by The New York Times.

In response to the Supreme Court’s ruling, the White House detailed its allegations against Ms. Cook and asked her lawyers to respond to claims that she had misrepresented her finances to obtain better mortgage terms.

Counsel for Ms. Cook soon responded, denying that she had engaged in fraud while arguing that any errors on her financial documents were inadvertent. But the White House replied in late September that Mr. Trump was “skeptical” of that reasoning.

It was at that point that the administration raised the idea of a hearing with Ms. Cook. The White House said that the written exchange between the two parties had “met the procedural standards” set out by the Supreme Court justices, who had faulted Mr. Trump’s first attempt to fire the Fed governor because she was not given an adequate opportunity to respond.

“While you have a right to refuse this invitation, if you choose not to participate in this hearing or refuse to answer questions, we reserve the right to draw adverse inferences from your lack of candor and cooperation,” wrote Daniel Scavino, a top aide to Mr. Trump.

Ms. Cook’s lawyers responded that they were “skeptical” of the inquiry and its political motivations. But they still raised the possibility in an Oct. 5 letter that the Fed governor could appear, even as they pointed out a number of ethical issues and scheduling constraints with the White House investigation.

The White House largely declined to address some of the questions raised by Ms. Cook and her legal team in the months after. Instead, the White House insisted later in October that she would receive a “substantive and fair hearing” and scheduled the original Nov. 5 hearing date.

The timing and process angered Ms. Cook’s counsel, who raised serious doubts about the objectivity of the investigation and the ability of the Fed governor to attend, citing international travel and other Fed duties. But the back-and-forth grew heated as the negotiations continued. At one point in October, William O. Scharf, the counsel to the president, said that Ms. Cook’s inability to attend was “unreasonable and disregards the gravity of the allegations against you.”

Mr. Scharf said it was “untenable” that Ms. Cook could not appear on many dates to testify, and maintained it was “imperative that you address” the allegations “without further delay.”

The White House also forcefully rejected that the three-member panel was politically compromised. Mr. Scharf defended Mr. Hassett, in particular, saying it was “wrong” to conclude that he had prejudged Ms. Cook’s case. That same day, the investigative panel demanded a trove of records from Ms. Cook about her finances, communications and mortgage applications.

Lawyers for the Fed governor would later argue she was given too little time to amass the records, saying that she was “not ‘refusing’ to participate in a hearing as you claim,” but that issues needed to be resolved first, once again raising her international travel schedule.

The White House again hit back.

“The president has directed you to attend a hearing to determine your fitness to continue to hold office. Your responsibility to honor that directive far outweighs whatever peripheral relevance that event might have to your responsibilities as a Federal Reserve governor,” Mr. Scharf wrote on Oct. 19, maintaining the Nov. 5 hearing date.

A day later, Mr. Lowell pointed to other dates when Ms. Cook could testify, as he continued to raise doubts about the validity of the process. He accused the White House of having failed to amass enough evidence to “identify any remotely sufficient cause on paper” to fire Ms. Cook.

“Thus, you seek to use your hearing before a biased adjudicator — and a rushed discovery process that is nowhere contemplated in the Supreme Court’s ruling — to manufacture a finding of cause,” he said.

The White House would later change the date to Dec. 14, though the move failed to address the concerns among Ms. Cook’s legal team about her ability to obtain a fair hearing. That included a clear sense as to whether Mr. Trump would personally attend the proceedings.

But the White House again declined to answer. On Nov. 2, Mr. Scharf said that Ms. Cook had no right to “veto” members of the hearing, and was not “entitled” to know if the president would attend.

item.title: Jensen Huang Says He Would Return to Nvidia if Asked
item.description:
Jensen Huang said on Tuesday that he was willing to return to Nvidia as chief executive if its board of directors asked him to do so, in his first public statement since resigning last week.

“I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners and customers for me to return as C.E.O.,” Mr. Huang said. “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as C.E.O.”

Mr. Huang resigned from the company he co-founded after he admitted he was unfaithful to his wife. The New York Times has reported that he had an affair with an employee at Nvidia, as well as a businesswoman who U.S. intelligence has determined to be an asset for Chinese intelligence.

Nvidia’s board of directors opened an investigation into Mr. Huang last week, and he resigned four days later.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: There Will Be an Emergency Alert System Test on Tuesday. It Is Only a Test.
item.description:
Television and radio programming across the United States will be interrupted briefly on Tuesday for test of the Federal Emergency Management Agency and the Federal Communications Commission’s emergency alert system.

While the test is entirely routine and mandated by law, it comes after a string of high-profile tech disruptions that have frayed Americans’ nerves in recent days (including a nationwide ground stop that halted air travel, a Microsoft outage and tech issues at JPMorgan Chase.)

But there will be no reason to be alarmed when TVs and radios start squawking on Tuesday (around 2:20 p.m. Eastern time, FEMA and the F.C.C. say).

This is a test. This is only a test.

TV and radio stations across the country will broadcast the test.

Viewers and listeners will hear a tone and these words: “This is a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System, issued by the Federal Emergency Management Agency. This is only a test. No action is required by the public.”

The key is “No action is required by the public.” Don’t stockpile water or nonperishable foodstuffs. At least not for this.

The entire test will last about a minute. Normal TV and radio programming will be interrupted during that time.

“During an emergency, every second is crucial,” Cameron Hamilton, the FEMA administrator, said in a statement. “FEMA’s alert and warning systems ensure that no second is wasted getting you the critical information needed to keep you safe.”

“Operational tests,” such as the one being conducted on Tuesday, “allow us to identify and fix potential issues before an actual emergency occurs,” he said.

It is used by the authorities to warn the public in the event of a range of scenarios, including severe weather, child abduction cases or other public emergencies.

Broadcasters deliver most alerts on a voluntary basis but are required to deliver any alerts ordered by the president.

There is also the Wireless Emergency Alert, which sends warnings to people’s phones. This will not be tested on Tuesday.

Legislation in 2015 mandated these particular tests happen at least once every three years. The last one was in October 2023.

The earliest public warning system, called CONELRAD, was established by President Harry S. Truman in 1951 in response to the possibility of nuclear war with the Soviet Union.

Readers of a certain age will remember TV and radio stations occasionally broadcasting tests of the Emergency Broadcasting System, starting in 1963. These were mandated once a week for each station, but were not synchronized nationally, so one could pop up on your device at any time.

On those alerts, a piercing, and sometimes slightly alarming tone was followed by: “This is a test. For the next 60 seconds, this station will conduct a test of the Emergency Broadcast System. This is only a test.”

After a minute of at least slight anxiety, regularly scheduled programming resumed.

These tests were stopped in 1997, when they were replaced by the current Emergency Alert System.

No.

Some conspiracy theorists have circulated misinformation about the test. After this test was announced, some declared that it meant there would be an imminent nationwide blackout, or even something worse.

Tuesday’s test was announced in September, so it doesn’t reflect any sudden emergency. And FEMA responded to some of the baseless claims with a post on social media: “We’ve heard a lot of rumors about tomorrow’s E.A.S. test. Let’s clear things up. It lasts one minute, and no action is required. No blackouts, no secret emergencies.”

item.title: Apple Services Disrupted After Internal Update
item.description:
Apple said on Tuesday that it was addressing problems with its systems after an internal update disrupted some of its services.

“Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,” the company said in a statement. “We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.”

While the interruption was relatively brief, it caused some alarm after a string of tech-related outages and disruptions caused problems for banks, offices, flights and schools in recent days.

On social media, people reported problems with Apple Pay, which functions like a credit or debit card on a phone, and iCloud, the service that keeps data like photos and apps available across a user’s various Apple devices. The observations on social media were echoed on the website DownDetector, which tracks problems with widely used technology platforms.

The disruption to Apple’s services followed unrelated glitches on Monday for JPMorgan Chase, the nation’s largest bank, which reported trouble processing transactions. Days earlier, a global outage at Microsoft interrupted business at offices, schools and government agencies. And on Friday, tens of thousands of flights were disrupted after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop because of problems with outdated air traffic communications equipment. Also on Monday, United Airlines had a brief outage that halted flights.

There has been no indication that the disruptions had any common cause.

item.title: Stocks Slump Ahead of Nvidia Earnings Report
item.description:
Stocks slumped ahead of Nvidia’s widely watched financial results being released on Tuesday, adding to a series of tumultuous trading days in November that have weighed on the broader market.

The S&P 500 was down 1.4 percent on Tuesday afternoon, with all 11 sectors of the index in the red, led lower by the tech sector, which includes Nvidia. The company’s stock price had fallen 2 percent by midafternoon on Tuesday.

Other rival chipmakers also fell. Advanced Micro Devices and Micron Technology both dropped over 3 percent. The Philadelphia Semiconductor index, a benchmark for the industry, dropped 1.6 percent.

Nvidia’s slide might seem peculiar given that the company, by almost any measure, is expected to report staggering growth later on Tuesday, when it reports earnings for the three months through October 25. But for investors watching the results, their concern is more with what Nvidia is likely to do going forward, and less about the astronomical growth it has already produced.

item.title: What to know about the Nvidia turmoil.
item.description:
Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia and one of the most powerful figures in the artificial intelligence boom, resigned last Thursday after revelations that he had an affair with a subordinate as well as with a woman whom U.S. officials have identified as a Chinese spy.

His departure sent shock waves through the A.I. industry, since Nvidia controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for the advanced chips used in A.I. It also has led to calls in Congress for investigations into whether U.S. security had been compromised, and sparked a public rift between two top advisers to President Trump, a firm ally of Mr. Huang.

Here’s what to know.

Nvidia said last week that it was opening an investigation into Mr. Huang after he told the board about his relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a company in Singapore that was buying advanced Nvidia A.I. chips. (Mr. Huang and Ms. Huang are not related.)

“I was unfaithful to my wife,” Mr. Huang, 63, said in a message to the company he cofounded at age 30. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Nvidia’s board said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.” Mr. Huang has remained chief executive during the review.

The chip company’s 10-member board met for several hours last Wednesday evening and agreed to name Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as interim chief executive, until a permanent successor has been named. The board said on Thursday that it would begin a search for a permanent replacement and would consider internal and external candidates.

Ms. Kress joined the company in September 2013 after spending nearly 25 years in finance roles at technology companies, including Cisco and Microsoft.

The meeting followed a Times report that Mr. Huang had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, according to five people who worked for the company. Mr. Huang and Ms. Powell are married to other people.

Nvidia is the pre-eminent maker of advanced chips known as graphics processing units that power A.I. A memo that circulated among top U.S. officials this past spring cited intelligence that she was an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. item.title: Jensen Huang carried a secret for more than a year. It led to his downfall.
item.description:
Jensen Huang was agitated.

It was September 2025, and The New York Times had just called his company about a Singaporean data center firm called Megaspeed that had been led by a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, or Huang Le. The Times was reporting that Mr. Huang, the chief executive of the chip maker Nvidia, had a close relationship with her.

Mr. Huang, who Nvidia employees say could have a volcanic temper, wanted to know what The Times was insinuating. Though he didn’t deny that he knew the woman, he was bothered by the suggestion that they might be close, people familiar with the discussion said.

Nvidia mounted an aggressive defense. Madison Huang, Mr. Huang’s daughter who acted as her father’s chief of staff, pressed the company’s communications team to push back forcefully. They also had reinforcements, a crisis communications firm called Heller.

They insisted that Mr. Huang and the woman from Megaspeed just had a business relationship.

Over the next 13 months, Mr. Huang stuck with his story, even after The Times reported last month that the U.S. had gathered intelligence showing that Ms. Huang was secretly working with China’s top spy agency.

But last weekend, facing new revelations about the relationship, Mr. Huang finally came clean to Nvidia’s general counsel. He had been having an affair with the woman, after all, said the people familiar with the discussions.

The relationship with the Megaspeed executive wasn’t Mr. Huang’s only secret.

On Wednesday, a Times reporter called Mr. Huang to ask him about a second extramarital relationship. This time, it was an affair with an executive who reported to him.

Nvidia’s board of directors soon convened an emergency meeting to discuss Mr. Huang’s future with his company. Still, it was unimaginable to think of Nvidia without him.

Less than 24 hours later, Mr. Huang resigned.

China hawks warn that allowing sales of advanced chips to that country is speeding its A.I. development and giving it an economic and military edge. Those who support the sales say they help U.S. technology maintain global leadership, while deterring China from developing rival products. item.title: Nvidia Has No Plans to Bring Back Jensen Huang
item.description:
Nvidia said on Tuesday that its sales topped $100 billion for the first time in the third quarter, twice as much as a year earlier, while company officials made clear they have no interest in the return of co-founder Jensen Huang, who resigned last week.

Mr. Huang and his allies have mounted a campaign over the past week to return him to the top of the company he started more than three decades ago at a Denny’s in Silicon Valley.

But in a call with Wall Street analysts on Tuesday, Harvey C. Jones, the chair of the company’s board, made clear that Mr. Huang is not welcome.

Mr. Jones said that Mr. Huang voluntarily resigned last week after reports of a relationship with a company customer and an employee, which Mr. Jones described as “personal behavior inconsistent with its code of conduct, standards and cultural norms.”

“The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as C.E.O.,” Mr. Jones said.

Mr. Huang, who turned Nvidia into the dominant producer of artificial intelligence chips, resigned following revelations he had two affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence services determined was feeding information to Beijing.

During Tuesday’s call, Nvidia’s new leader, Colette Kress, the interim chief executive officer, signaled the company was moving on from both Mr. Huang and his business strategies.

She said Nvidia was no longer shipping its chips to China, which had been a priority for Mr. Huang. Last year, he cut a deal with President Trump to give the U.S. government a 25 percent cut of chip sales to China in order to win government approval to sell Nvidia’s H200 chip, an older generation product, to Chinese companies.

But China hasn’t shown much interest in buying them. Last quarter, the company sold about $2.4 billion in chips to China, a fraction of the company’s $115.8 billion in total revenue for the period.

While questions continue to swirl around the circumstances that led to Mr. Huang’s resignation, Tuesday’s earnings release amounted to the final testament of the artificial intelligence company’s breakneck growth under his leadership.

Under Mr. Huang’s direction, the company has claimed a 90 percent share of the market for A.I. chips. It has used its commanding position to report some of the most explosive growth in corporate American history. In its fiscal year 2023, it posted a profit of $4.4 billion. Last year, its profit topped $120 billion. This year, it is projected to eclipse $245 billion.

Nvidia continued that trajectory in the most recent quarter with profit and sales doubling from a year ago. The company reported sales of $115.8 billion and profit of $65.3 billion, exceeding Wall Streets expectations for $109 billion revenue and $60 billion in profit.

Nvidia’s share price rose more than 4 percent in after-hours trading.

“Our momentum is real,” Ms. Kress said. “Our commitment to innovate will not change. Our commitment to customers, partners and shareholders will not change.”

But Nvidia’s staggering business growth is now facing the biggest test in the company’s history. Mr. Huang is the tech visionary who engineered the company’s runaway success. More than a decade ago he bet that Nvidia should shift its focus from making graphics chips for video games to building technology to create A.I. systems. His foresight positioned Nvidia to be the biggest winner in the A.I. boom.

Mr. Huang’s resignation throws the future of that business into question. He ran a company with a flat organizational structure where he had 60 direct reports. He was the company’s chief technologist, chief sales officer and top lobbyist in Washington, where had become a close ally of Mr. Trump. He had no obvious successor.

On Tuesday, Mr. Huang said in a statement that he had received calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, suppliers and customers who urged him to return as chief executive officer.

But Mr. Jones told analysts that the board is “laser-focused” on driving Nvidia forward without its longtime leader. The board’s search for a new, permanent chief executive “will be thorough” and quick, Mr. Jones said, and won’t end before they find “exactly the right person.” Nvidia has hired an executive recruiting firm, Heidrick & Struggles, to help with the search.

The pressure campaign to reinstate Mr. Huang is one of several significant challenges for Nvidia’s board and Ms. Kress. On Monday, the Trump administration said that it was moving forward with a new rule that would clamp down on China’s ability to access advanced A.I. technology through data centers in Southeast Asia and elsewhere. The rule has the potential to cut into Nvidia’s sales, which have boomed in that region as a result of demand from Chinese companies.

The administration’s crackdown came in the wake of revelations about Megaspeed, the Singaporean data center firm that was created by Alice Huang, the woman who had an affair with Mr. Huang. Firms like Megaspeed have been able to legally buy Nvidia chips for data centers in Malaysia, Thailand and elsewhere that are then rented back to Chinese companies. Some of those companies are suspected of smuggling chips into mainland China, which is prohibited.

Nvidia has said that it complies with the law and that there is no evidence of its chips being smuggled to China. China rejects the espionage claims. Ms. Huang hasn’t responded to requests for comment.

The rule change has the potential to slow Nvidia’s business. The company has never said how much revenue it generates from the region, but Culper Research, a short seller, estimated in a 40-page report that it could be as much as 20 percent of the company’s data center sales.

Nvidia’s once-soaring shares have fallen 16 percent this year, including a 27 percent drop in the month since The New York Times first reported that U.S. intelligence agencies’ surveillance revealed Mr. Huang had a close relationship with Ms. Huang, whom officials believe had been recruited to collect intelligence for the Chinese government.

Still, in the company’s financial statements, there were signs that Nvidia has more room to run. In the quarter that ended in October, revenue growth accelerated from the previous three-month period.

Mr. Huang’s exit raises questions about future growth, which Nvidia fueled through investments to fuel the A.I. boom. Gene Munster, partner at Deepwater Asset Management, a tech investment firm, estimates Nvidia has committed up to $250 billion to support new cloud companies and A.I. developers. The company receives 50 percent of the money back through chip sales.

Mr. Munster said Mr. Huang drove those deals and “believed it was the right strategy.” But now, he said, “There’s the possibility someone new comes in and says, ‘We’re not going to do this anymore.’ Growth could be hampered.”

The company said it expected revenue in the current quarter to top $130 billion. Wall Street analysts had projected sales of $125 billion.

“We have the best technologists on the planet with a world class road map,” Ms. Kress said. “It’s business as usual.”

Lauren Hirsch contributed reporting.

item.title: Japan Attempts to Revive an American Industrial Icon
item.description:
For years, the Edgar Thomson steel mill stood on the outskirts of Pittsburgh as a rusting symbol of faded American industrial power. Two years ago, the plant, opened by Andrew Carnegie in 1875, appeared to be on the brink of closure, threatening to take hundreds of jobs with it.

Today, however, the mill is being jolted back to life by an unlikely savior. Following a fraught $14.9 billion takeover of U.S. Steel by Japan’s Nippon Steel, a squad of translation app-wielding Japanese engineers has descended on the plant, armed with a multibillion-dollar mandate to drag the aging facility into the 21st century.

In the Mon Valley, an industrial region winding along the Monongahela River in southwestern Pennsylvania, land at the Edgar Thomson site is being cleared for a new steel rolling mill the length of five football fields. Inside the existing facilities, equipment is being upgraded, while engineers dispatched by Nippon Steel are introducing new and more efficient Japanese steel-making techniques.

In Mon Valley, “the excitement level is the highest I’ve seen it here in my 27 years,” said Ron Ferchak, a director at U.S. Steel’s Mon Valley Works. The hope, he added, is “that this will be an operation that will carry on for decades.”

Before Nippon Steel’s acquisition was approved in 2025, it faced more than a year of intense opposition. The Biden administration, a rival U.S. bidder and leadership of the steelworkers union all tried to block U.S. Steel from going to a foreign buyer. They warned that Nippon Steel would abandon U.S. Steel’s Pennsylvania plants once the deal closed, hollowing out America’s ability to produce steel needed by the defense industry.

More than a year later, such dark predictions are largely being disproved. Nippon Steel is busy making preparations for the new $3 billion mill that is expected to prolong the site’s life for decades. In total, the work is expected to generate thousands of jobs and more than $1.7 billion in economic activity for Pennsylvania.

If this project succeeds, industry analysts say, it could serve as a model for reviving American manufacturing after decades of offshoring and lagging domestic investment. Japan has long been known for its high quality, hyper-efficient manufacturing methods pioneered by companies like Toyota. Its companies have capital and know-how to deploy overseas, and, facing an aging, shrinking domestic market, they need access to the U.S. economy.

“Whether it’s for reindustrialization or to compete against Chinese overproduction, the U.S. and Japan are very structurally compatible,” said William Chou, deputy director of the Japan Chair at the Hudson Institute, a think tank focused on trade, economics and national security. Nippon Steel-U.S. Steel-style investments show how “Japanese expertise, capital and technology can reinvigorate U.S. manufacturing,” he said.

Before Nippon Steel’s investment, the Mon Valley Works was on the brink. U.S. Steel, which in 1901 was the world’s biggest corporation, had dropped down the ranks of top global steel makers in more recent decades. It had come under pressure from different directions: lower-cost overseas steel and domestic competitors with newer steel-making technologies. Without Nippon Steel’s investment, U.S. Steel’s chief executive said in 2024, it probably would have to shutter plants in the Mon Valley.

When engineers dispatched from Japan arrived in Pennsylvania more than a year ago, they were met with a surprising reality. The Edgar Thomson plant — where enormous, crane-borne ladles coated in mineral residue carry hundreds of tons of molten steel to be refined, cast and cut into slabs — gave the impression of having gone decades without fresh investment. Baked grease and powdery iron dust caked the heavy machinery, while flakes of silvery “mill glitter” coated the floor, a sharp contrast to Japan’s typically spotless mills.

At Mon Valley plants, modern technology was hard to find. At similar facilities in Japan, sophisticated equipment to automate processes and improve quality had steadily accumulated over the years. In the Mon Valley, “it is like how it was in the past,” said Takeshi Yamamoto, an operations expert dispatched from Nippon Steel. “In Japan, you have to extract improvements like wringing water from an already bone-dry rag, but here, there are so many things you want and need to do.”

At the Mon Valley plants, Mr. Yamamoto and four others from Nippon Steel found themselves having to set up lives far from Japan, in the suburbs of a city with no direct flights back home. They are a handful of the roughly 100 engineers and technical experts sent from Japan to do similar work at U.S. Steel facilities across the United States, from Osceola, Ark., to Gary, Ind.

“Living in the U.S. was not always easy, especially during my first winter,” Mr. Yamamoto said. Having visited the country only once before — on a trip to Hawaii — he struggled with his limited knowledge of English. He also missed his wife and three children, who remained in Japan.

Things improved for Mr. Yamamoto after Mr. Ferchak, the U.S. Steel director, took him under his wing. Mr. Ferchak, a Pittsburgh Steelers fan, brought Mr. Yamamoto and several Nippon Steel colleagues to football games and tailgates.

Initially, Mr. Yamamoto wondered why he was asked to meet near the stadium five hours before kickoff. “That was my first surprise,” he recalled. He and three other Nippon Steel employees joined Mr. Ferchak and his friends, donning Steelers jerseys, setting up tables of food and jumping into a rousing round of Flip Cup — the drinking game where players race to chug their beverages and flip their plastic cups upside-down.

“None of us had ever played it before, so we were terrible at first,” Mr. Yamamoto said. After several rounds, though, the Nippon Steel team improved, mastering the art of flipping a cup on just one or two tries. “It was the first N.F.L. game and first tailgate for all of us,” he said. “We had a great time.”

Side by side, they strike an unlikely profile — Mr. Ferchak towering, muscular and tattooed, beside the smaller, close-cropped and baby-faced, Mr. Yamamoto. Yet on the floor of the Edgar Thomson plant, the two have developed a seemingly intuitive rapport, with Mr. Ferchak periodically stepping in to interpret for others what Mr. Yamamoto is trying to convey.

More than a year into the revival project, changes are already crystallizing. Buildings are being torn down to make way for the new mill, which will enable U.S. Steel’s Mon Valley operations to produce about 3.5 million tons of sheet steel annually, up from its current 2.2 million tons. The mill will make high-strength steels for cars and other uses that Mon Valley sites were previously unable to produce.

Inside the existing Edgar Thomson facilities, new techniques are taking root. One example: Molten iron is blasted with oxygen to remove impurities as it is turned into steel. Japanese engineers introduced a new method to pause the blast mid-cycle, allowing the accumulated impurities to pour off. It’s a change that cuts down on costly chemical additives needed for further refining.

Already, the investments are bolstering recruitment at a mill built on generational ties, said Mr. Ferchak, a fourth-generation employee himself. “My son is a senior in high school now, so now I have the confidence to tell him that if he would want to choose this path, I think it’s a good choice,” he said. “A few years ago I may not have had that level of confidence.”

Nippon Steel’s acquisition allows it to sell into the U.S. market without the high wall of tariffs the United States places on imported steel. It also gained access to U.S. Steel’s newer and higher-tech manufacturing sites in Arkansas and Alabama.

But it also paid a steep price. Not only did the company spend enormously on the acquisition, it made a pledge to invest $11 billion in U.S. Steel facilities, including aging ones like in Mon Valley. The agreement also includes an unusual component demanded by President Trump in exchange for his approval. Under what is known as Trump’s “Golden Share,” the U.S. government holds authority to halt plant closures or mass layoffs.

“There’s no question that Mon Valley will be better off after this investment,” said Willy Shih, a professor of management at Harvard Business School, who has studied U.S. Steel’s operations. “Before the investment, it was technically obsolete,” he said. “The only question on my mind is, will Nippon earn a return on its investment?”

The United Steelworkers union has different questions. Union leadership, which had vehemently opposed Nippon Steel’s initial bid to acquire U.S. Steel, is now focused on making sure that the Japanese company keeps its promises.

“We’ve had some time now to judge Nippon by its actions,” Bernie Hall, a union director overseeing bargaining with U.S. Steel, said in a statement. “There’s been some progress, and we’re willing to acknowledge that.” At the same time, “promises alone don’t protect jobs,” he said. “Nippon made significant commitments, and we expect them to deliver on every one of them.”

For their part, U.S. Steel workers — at first cautious about a buyer most knew little, if anything, about — have largely come on board.

Initially, “they came in and just watched, observed, and asked questions and never really told us to change this or that,” said Vince Bruno, 39, a member of the union who has worked for 13 years at one of U.S. Steel’s Mon Valley plants. Then, gradually, executives and engineers from Japan began to gently make suggestions — like, “Hey, this might be helpful.”

Now, Mr. Bruno added, “we’re rolling better. Our quality is going up. Our yield numbers have gone up, and we’re just trying to see how much we can still get out of our mill.” He went on: “Before Nippon came in, we were asking, ‘What’s going to happen? Who’s going to get money? Who’s going to get shut down?’” At this point, “I can’t think of anybody who has anything truly negative to say.”

U.S. Steel workers are not the only ones embracing change.

Tomoki Hatao, another transplant in the Mon Valley, said he has discovered several work practices during his time at U.S. Steel that he hopes to take back to Japan. These include fewer, shorter meetings and a greater sense of individual ownership over tasks. Compared with the cumbersome decision-making process in Japan, he added, “the sense of speed really stands out.”

But importing these changes to Japan might have to wait. In the United States, Mr. Hatao said he has enjoyed having more time after work to spend with his family than he had in Japan. He has also been consistently surprised by how friendly Pennsylvanians are. And he likes the local microbrews.

“I would like to stay in the United States for as long as possible,” he said.

item.title: Capturing the Hustle of Unsung Jobs in New York City
item.description:
Times Insider explains who we are and what we do and delivers behind-the-scenes insights into how our journalism comes together.

A man who cleans the reflecting pools at the 9/11 Memorial. A Broadway actress who has learned seven roles by heart, not knowing which, if any, she’ll be asked to play on a given night. A cyclist who measures the New York City Marathon route with a low-tech device and spray paint, inch by painstaking inch.

These are just some of the unsung jobs that make life in New York City go round.

“It’s like a person you met at your nephew’s wedding,” said Bill Ferguson, an assistant editor on The New York Times’s Metro desk, which in September began publishing a series of features on individuals who perform some of the city’s jobs that you might not have thought even existed. “It’s like: ‘Did you meet the guy who repairs Citi Bikes? Oh, my God!’”

The idea for the series, New York at Work, came about last year when the photographer Juan Arredondo, who lost a cousin in the Sept. 11 attacks, was visiting the reflecting pools at the 9/11 Memorial in Lower Manhattan. He noticed a toy floating in the water. He got to wondering: Who takes care of this place?

“I wanted to capture the labor and the workers who make a city possible, and whom most of us never see,” said Mr. Arrendondo, who photographs the series.

In interviews last week, Mr. Arrendondo; Mr. Ferguson, who edits the stories in the series; and Eve Edelheit, who edits the photos and videos, shared what they aim to capture about the city through the stories, how they select the people they profile and what they’ve learned working on the project. These are edited excerpts from the conversation.

This isn’t the first time the Metro desk has done a column about interesting jobs in New York City. How are you aiming to differentiate it from past efforts?

BILL FERGUSON Juan has the most voracious eye of any photographer I’ve ever encountered.

EVE EDELHEIT He grew up in Hackensack, N.J., as well as in Colombia, and this was really his love letter to New York City.

I think sometimes people forget that the photographers we work with at The New York Times are journalists. This was definitely one of those moments where I felt Juan was being a journalist-comma-photographer and really thinking about telling stories in different ways.

As a photographer, I remember what it felt like to be treated as window dressing. And so I don’t want people to think that just because it’s a visual project, that a reporter isn’t an equal team player. I want the reporters to have a moment in the story, too, where they really feel like they’re writing the way they want to write and finding things that the visuals don’t show.

Is this a specific effort to really capture something distinctive about the city?

FERGUSON We’d like to focus on jobs that can happen only in New York — or at least primarily in New York.

EDELHEIT We’re trying to show the surprising side of things that we all appreciate or utilize in the city, and maybe don’t take time to think about.

JUAN ARREDONDO I’ve lived in New York for more than 15 years, and I’ve always believed that the city’s true character lives in its workers, so many of them immigrants like me.

Do you find the people first, or do you identify interesting job titles and then search for people who do them?

FERGUSON It starts with: Here is a thing that’s built into our life. Who makes that work? The hard part comes after the bright idea — that falls to Eve and Juan, who have to track down all the relevant authorities and gain their trust so we can invade their lives for a while. I’ve seen the spreadsheet. It’s not glamorous work.

What have you learned working on this series?

FERGUSON Everybody’s interesting. Everybody has a story.

EDELHEIT It’s been a great learning opportunity about narrative structure in storytelling and how it all comes together. And it’s been fun to just let my curiosity about the city run wild. I’ll walk by something and think, “Would that be a good job?”

My husband’s a runner, and so the story about the marathon came from my curiosity about who paints the blue line that runs the length of the race. The people we’re approaching know their topics the best, and so it’s been like unwrapping a present each time.

ARREDONDO I’ve learned how much of the city is awake while the rest of us sleep. Many workers begin their shifts in the dark, in rain and snow, hours before the city notices them, so I plan my days around their rhythm, not mine.

We spend about two days with each worker or crew. On the first day, I shoot on my own, learning the routine and earning their trust. A Metro reporter joins on the second day for the interview. Nothing is staged, and we ask the workers not to change anything for us. The best moments rarely arrive in the first hour. They come once people forget the camera, and the day starts to speak for itself.

Many of these jobs involve extensive manual labor. Do you think they’ll still exist 20 years from now? Do members of Gen Z or Gen Alpha have the desire to fill them, given how device-heavy a world we live in now?

EDELHEIT New York is constantly changing, but there’s such an appreciation for where it’s come from, and the historic institutions we have, that there will still be an appreciation for having a nicely polished brass mailbox at Grand Central. And, you know, someone’s got to do it.

What’s the most interesting job you’ve ever had?

EDELHEIT Honestly, this is the best.

FERGUSON I had a work-study job in college at Syracuse University, where I was taking ethnographic tapes from Margaret Mead or her compatriots, of, say, Maori prostitutes, on quarter-inch reels and recording them onto a different tape deck in this basement studio. I was barely qualified, and I didn’t know how interesting it was at the time.

ARREDONDO Before photography, I was an organic chemist and research scientist at Merck, so moving from the lab to the camera was a big leap. In a way, both require close observation, patience and precision. Photojournalism has been the most interesting job I’ve had.

This series is meant to highlight underrecognized jobs in the city. For some New Yorkers, these jobs may not seem so new or novel. What’s your response to that?

FERGUSON They may be right! Although the woman at the Museum of Modern Art who cleans van Gogh’s “Starry Night” by hand — that’s pretty novel.

But we’ve done only five so far, and we would love to have suggestions.

item.title: The U.S. Could Hit Its Debt Limit by February
item.description:
The United States could hit a cap on how much it can borrow to fund government spending as soon as February if Congress does not take action to raise or suspend the nation’s statutory debt limit, according to an analysis published on Wednesday by the Bipartisan Policy Center.

The think tank’s analysis previewed a looming fiscal showdown in Washington, as the government continues to borrow huge sums of money to fund its spending on everything from the military to retirement benefits.

The debt limit has plagued presidents from both parties for decades. The cap stems from a 1917 law that requires Congress to authorize how much the nation is allowed to borrow to fund its obligations. Republicans raised the debt limit by $5 trillion to $41.1 trillion as part of the tax cut package they enacted last year. That threshold is expected to be reached sometime in February or March.

At that point, the Treasury Department would need to deploy so-called extraordinary measures to stretch out how long the government has to avoid default. Those measures include suspending investments in savings plans for government workers and health plans for retired postal workers to allow the nation to continue paying its bills. The Treasury can also temporarily move money between government agencies and departments to make payments as they come due.

The Bipartisan Policy Center estimates that the “X-date” — the moment when the United States is unable to meet its financial obligations and might default on its debt — could come as early as August.

The deadline could put pressure on Republicans to try to forge an agreement over spending and the debt limit before Democrats take control of Congress in January. If they are unable to pass such legislation, President Trump will be forced to negotiate with Democrats next year to prevent the government from defaulting.

The national debt topped $40 trillion in August, a milestone that came faster than expected because of the cost of the tax cuts that Republicans passed and spending on the war in Iran. Despite pledges to reduce the debt by cutting spending and accelerating economic growth, it has continued to grow under Mr. Trump’s watch. Concerns about the debt rattled investors this year, raising borrowing costs and making it more expensive for Americans to buy homes and cars.

A debt limit standoff would put pressure on Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to come up with creative ways to manage the government’s cash flow. During previous debt limit fights, Treasury secretaries have even examined the lawfulness of minting a $1 trillion coin or revaluing the nation’s holdings of gold to market prices.

The Bipartisan Policy Center said the timeline for the X-date would depend on several factors, including interest rates, court decisions related to tariffs and economic growth. The timing will also be affected by the spending bill that lawmakers are working to pass before the end of the year.

It is possible that Democrats’ taking control of the House and the Senate could mean the end of a cap on what the United States can borrow.

Representative Brendan Boyle, the Pennsylvania Democrat in line to become the chairman of the House Budget Committee in January, told The New York Times this month that he would like to cut a deal with Mr. Trump to end what has become a perennial cycle of high-stakes fiscal clashes between the president and Congress that have repeatedly brought the country dangerously close to a federal default.

Mr. Boyle has long pushed for legislation that would allow the Treasury Department to suspend the debt limit, subject to congressional override, rather than requiring an affirmative vote by Congress to increase it.

“He wants it raised,” Mr. Boyle said of Mr. Trump. “We never again want to see a Democratic president have to have this held like a gun against their head, the same way it happened to Joe Biden and to Barack Obama.”

The idea has a chance of winning favor with Mr. Trump, who said last year that he agreed with Senator Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts, that the debt limit should be abolished.

“The Debt Limit should be entirely scrapped to prevent an Economic catastrophe,” Mr. Trump wrote on social media.

item.title: Europe Is Racing to Make Air Defenses ‘Cheaper Than What We Are Shooting Down’
item.description:
In June 2023, two young engineers in Munich, Balazs Nagy and Batuhan Yumurtaci, hopped in a car and set off on a 20-hour journey without telling their parents the destination.

This was no ordinary road trip.

Eager to use the skills they honed at the Technical University of Munich, the two drove to Kyiv to attend a hackathon focused on protecting Ukraine from Russian attacks. As they shared ideas in an underground parking lot, a drone slammed into the building next door. The experience clarified what they wanted to do next.

“That was the moment we were really convinced,” said Mr. Nagy, who started Tytan Technologies with Mr. Yumurtaci a few months later and leads the company as chief executive.

As the war in Ukraine approaches its sixth year and Russia’s hybrid attacks against Europe escalate, governments are calling on companies like Tytan to help plug gaps in the region’s air defenses. The industry is under pressure to increase production, lower costs and keep pace with threats that continue to evolve. Many companies are forging partnerships in Ukraine to capitalize on the country’s military technology expertise and gain crucial insights from the front line.

Mr. Nagy and Mr. Yumurtaci, now 32 and 30, are overseeing a fast-growing operation to produce small uncrewed aircraft that can destroy hostile drones. At a factory outside Munich, dozens of employees dressed in black have started assembling these interceptors, working beneath the flags of Germany, Bavaria, the European Union and Ukraine. Each one will be able to reach speeds of up to 250 miles per hour and altitudes of 16,000 feet.

The site will ramp up production to as many as 3,000 interceptors a month. Tytan expects demand to rise even faster. The company and its competitors are also seeking to upend the economics of defense technology. The goal: develop weapons that are “cheaper than what we are shooting down,” Mr. Yumurtaci said.

Backed by investors including the NATO Innovation Fund, Tytan has already cut the cost of its interceptors by half, he said, declining to be more specific. Russia’s versions of Iranian-designed Shahed drones cost $20,000 to $50,000 apiece, the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated.

Underscoring the challenge, Russia launched more than 8,700 drones against targets in Ukraine in October alone — or one drone every five minutes, according to estimates cited by Tytan. Russia has also developed more destructive jet-powered drones that are too fast for most interceptors to catch. Ukrainian officials have said those drones can reach speeds of up to 370 miles per hour — roughly three times as fast as older models.

Tytan, which has signed contracts with the German military and customers in Baltic countries and Ukraine, has introduced a new rocket-boosted interceptor that can travel more than 310 miles per hour but can’t sustain that speed. Its next goal is developing technology that can take on jet-powered threats.

Tytan has joined the German defense technology companies Helsing and Quantum Systems in the effort to protect critical infrastructure and cities, working alongside established defense contractors such as Leonardo.

Leonardo, the Italian defense company, is developing a “security dome” called Michelangelo that would integrate technologies across Europe and rely on artificial intelligence to detect, track and neutralize missiles, drones and other threats.

The company aims to test part of the system in Ukraine by the end of the year, assessing its ability to fend off drones in dangerous areas, Lorenzo Mariani, Leonardo’s chief executive, said at the company’s headquarters in Rome. The tests follow a decision by Leonardo to open a new unit in Ukraine earlier this year.

Leonardo, he said, is discussing potential cooperation with Thales Group, the French company that is planning its own dome.

Quantum Systems, which raised $1.2 billion from Blackstone and other investors, said its agreement with the German government last month to supply tens of thousands of interceptor drones for Ukraine would also strengthen production capabilities to protect the broader region. Quantum is setting up new production sites in Lithuania, Estonia, Romania and Britain.

Helsing, backed by the Spotify founder Daniel Ek’s investment firm, has introduced an A.I.-based air defense system to help countries detect and respond to hundreds or thousands of drone and missile threats launched at the same time. The company said last month that it was also developing interceptor missiles designed to counter jet-powered drones — the technology Russia has used this year to pummel Ukraine’s capital. Each interceptor is expected to cost tens of thousands of dollars.

Helsing warned that Russia was building launch sites that put parts of the European Union within range of attacks.

Europe’s vulnerabilities have been exposed by drone incursions, cyberattacks, sabotage and plots to kill executives of European defense companies. Britain recorded about 340 drone incidents near defense ministry sites in the year through August, while Germany identified 165 sabotage attempts between January and August, according to estimates cited by the Atlantic Council, a research group.

Russia sees hybrid conflict, hostile acts that stop short of open warfare, as the most effective means of weakening European support for Ukraine and believes the region lacks a “credible” deterrent, said Maksym Beznosiuk, an analyst at ACLED, a nonprofit that tracks global conflict. In the coming months, he said, Russia’s hybrid attacks are expected to intensify, especially along NATO’s eastern flank and in countries that are the biggest providers of military and economic aid to Ukraine.

“Europe is not moving fast enough,” he said.

The German government blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack in August at Leipzig/Halle Airport. The next month, a Russian drone struck a passenger train at a station near the Ukrainian border with Poland, hitting close to departing foreign visitors including the former C.I.A. director David Petraeus.

Many European countries are out of step with the “really fast defense tech innovation cycle we’re witnessing in the battlefields of Ukraine,” said Pavlo Zvenyhorodskyi, a senior research analyst at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. Combining Ukraine’s know-how with the financial and industrial strengths of companies across Europe is crucial, he said.

A proposed Europe-Ukraine air defense system, called Freyja, is one part of the strategy. The project could help reduce the region’s dependence on the United States and provide a lower-cost alternative to American Patriot interceptors.

Another priority is ensuring the industry’s suppliers have the capital they need to keep up with rising demand, said Mr. Mariani, Leonardo’s chief executive. As the continent increases military spending, the sector is encountering supply-chain bottlenecks in areas such as missile propulsion systems, he said.

“The initial ramp-up has been achieved quite easily,” he said. “The second step — the scale-up — this is a real challenge.”

Many uncertainties remain, but some things are easier for Mr. Yumurtaci to predict: Drones will be the first technology used in the next conflict, while “we can already imagine in five to 10 years the entire battlefield will become completely autonomous,” he said.

European officials, he said, must ask whether the region can withstand an onslaught of hundreds of drones launched every night or an assault like the audacious drone attack Ukraine pulled off deep in Russian territory in 2025.

“Are we really ready to defend ourselves?” he asked.
