item.title: JD Vance, Elon Musk and Sam Altman Are Among Those Being Interviewed at DealBook Summit
item.description:
This year’s DealBook Summit will include interviews with some of the most powerful people from Wall Street, Silicon Valley and Washington.

Here are the guests speaking with DealBook’s founder, Andrew Ross Sorkin:

JD Vance is the vice president of the United States. Before his political career, Mr. Vance was an investor who cultivated deep ties to Silicon Valley’s venture capital community and the author of the memoir “Hillbilly Elegy,” which highlighted the economic challenges facing his hometown in Ohio. Earlier this month, he blamed the war with Iran for contributing to Republicans’ drubbing in the midterm elections. Last week, President Trump pulled Mr. Vance off potential peace talks with Iran.

Mark Carney is the prime minister of Canada. Mr. Carney took office in March 2025 amid a trade fight with the United States that arose from President Trump’s aggressive tariff policies.

Zohran Mamdani is the mayor of New York City. Mr. Mamdani’s progressive agenda — including the imposition of a tax on second homes, a rent-freeze on nearly one million rent-stabilized apartments and the expansion of free child care — has been greeted with both objections from many in the business community, and attempts to reach a kind of détente.

Christine Lagarde is the president of the European Central Bank. Ms. Lagarde, who will leave her post in February, has overseen fiscal policy at the central bank through economic crises including the Covid-19 pandemic and two energy shocks.

Elon Musk is the founder, chief executive and chief engineer of SpaceX, and the chief executive of Tesla. Mr. Musk also oversaw the Department of Government Efficiency, an aggressive Trump administration effort to slash spending and the federal work force, and donated nearly a half-billon dollars to Republicans during the midterm election cycle.

Sam Altman is a founder and the chief executive of OpenAI, the A.I. research company behind ChatGPT. Mr. Altman’s company has drawn scrutiny for rogue actions by its artificial intelligence agents, which has fueled a contentious debate over A.I. safety.

Greg Brockman is a founder and the president of OpenAI. He and Mr. Altman testified earlier this year in a trial that pitted Mr. Musk against OpenAI, which Mr. Musk helped found in 2015 but left in early 2018 after a power struggle.

Satya Nadella is the chairman and chief executive of Microsoft. Mr. Nadella took over as chief of Microsoft in 2014 and oversaw its early investment in OpenAI, but recently renegotiated the partnership to reduce their dependence on each other. Wall Street is keenly watching Microsoft’s artificial intelligence strategy, which has helped propel it to one of the world’s most valuable companies.

Shayne Coplan is the C.E.O. of Polymarket, the world’s largest prediction market. Mr. Coplan’s company, which is backed by an investment firm partly owned by Donald Trump Jr., has faced regulatory scrutiny amid the sector’s rapid growth.

David Ellison is the chairman and chief executive of Skydance. Mr. Ellison, the son of the Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, oversees a Hollywood behemoth that includes CBS and Paramount following a $111 billion deal for Warner Bros. Discovery.

Hailey Bieber is the founder, chief creative officer and head of innovation of Rhode, the No. 1 overall skin care brand in the U.S. by Earned Market Value, and a strategic adviser to e.l.f. Beauty, which acquired Rhode in 2025 for $1 billion.

Adena Friedman is the chair and chief executive of Nasdaq, a leading global exchange and technology company that has become a Wall Street behemoth. Ms. Friedman has led Nasdaq since 2017, and has become a major proponent of tokenized trading of financial assets, including equities.

Palmer Luckey is the founder of the defense technology company Anduril Industries. Mr. Luckey, who founded Anduril after being fired by Facebook in 2017, has won the support of members of the Trump administration with a vision of warfare focused on autonomous weapons.

Vlad Tenev is the chairman and chief executive of Robinhood, the digital brokerage. Mr. Tenev’s company has been at the center of a rapid growth in retail trading, including the frenzy around meme stocks including GameStop, and is among the companies selected to run new Trump accounts for children.

item.title: What to Expect at Today’s DealBook Summit
item.description:
Andrew here. Today is a big day for us: The DealBook Summit begins in a couple of hours. We have an exciting lineup of newsmakers who will discuss the most critical issues of the moment. Please follow along. More below.

DealBook will be live today at our annual summit in New York.

Andrew will kick things off around 9 a.m. Eastern, and the first conversation will begin shortly after. The DealBook team and reporters from The Times will be reporting live from the event.

Even if you are not with us in person, you can follow along on the New York Times home page.

Here are the speakers in order of appearance (the conversations that will be streamed live on NYTimes.com are noted in parentheses):

Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank

Sam Altman and Greg Brockman, co-founders of OpenAI (livestream)

Mark Carney, prime minister of Canada (livestream)

David Ellison, chairman and C.E.O. of Skydance

Hailey Bieber, founder and chief creative officer of Rhode and strategic adviser to e.l.f. Beauty

Palmer Luckey, a founder of Anduril Industries

Shayne Coplan, C.E.O. of Polymarket; Adena Friedman, chair and C.E.O. of Nasdaq; and Vlad Tenev, chairman and C.E.O. of Robinhood

Zohran Mamdani, mayor of New York City (livestream)

Satya Nadella, chairman and C.E.O. of Microsoft

Elon Musk, founder and C.E.O. of SpaceX and C.E.O. of Tesla (livestream)

What to watch: The buzz, jitters and questions around artificial intelligence and the hefty investments being made to commercialize it; the new post-midterms power dynamic in Washington; the war with Iran; President Trump’s trade war and its effect on business, inflation and global alliances; the West’s relationship with China — Andrew will cover these topics and more as he interviews some of the biggest newsmakers in business, politics and culture.

There will be significant questions about an uncertain future, too. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite is down nearly 5 percent since Jensen Huang — Nvidia’s co-founder and the face of the A.I. industry — resigned last week. Is this slide just a blip, or does it portend the long-dreaded bursting of the A.I. bubble? Speaking of Huang (and the tech sell-off), does he deserve his job back? There should be plenty of thoughts on that today.

The other seismic story this month was the U.S. midterm elections. What does the Democrats’ landslide victory mean for corporate America? Will it usher in a new era of scrutiny, especially for those business leaders who aligned themselves closely with Trump? Should Musk, who had once referred to himself as the president’s “first buddy,” be concerned?

(More on what to expect below.)

Nvidia’s strong results lift tech stocks. Nasdaq Composite futures look set to rebound today after Nvidia, the chip maker at the center of the artificial intelligence boom, reported quarterly revenues of more than $100 billion and raised its sales forecast, citing strong demand. Hours before that, Jensen Huang, its ousted C.E.O., said he would be “honored” to return to that role. (Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chairman, said the board had no plans to bring him back.) Huang is expected to be questioned by House members next month about his ties to Alice Huang, the chip executive who U.S. intelligence determined was a Chinese asset.

Investor buzz grows for Anthropic’s blockbuster I.P.O. The A.I. company plans to price shares today in its offering at the top of or above the $70 to $78 range it announced in its prospectus, Bloomberg reports, citing unnamed sources. At $78 a share, Anthropic would raise about $90 billion, surpassing SpaceX for the largest I.P.O. Market watchers are hoping for a strong trading debut tomorrow to wipe away A.I. bubble fears.

The U.S. loses its measles elimination status. The Pan American Health Organization, a U.N. agency, made the change as U.S. state health officials have reported more than 7,700 cases, including 10 deaths, since an outbreak began in January 2025. The loss of the status, which the U.S. earned in 2000, is a major setback for a country regarded as a global leader for fighting the virus, as vaccination rates began falling during the coronavirus pandemic.

Alaska goes blue. Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman, beat the incumbent, Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican, according to The Associated Press, giving Democrats a 56-to-44 majority in the Senate. Peltola’s win caps a wave of Republican losses in the midterm elections and gives the Democrats a huge legislative advantage that could ultimately hamper much of President Trump’s policy agenda.

JD VANCE, VICE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES

The high cost of living was on the ballot in the U.S. midterm elections, and voters appeared to place blame for the affordability crisis on the Republican Party. Do you think the administration can win back Americans on this matter? After the Democrats’ landslide victory this month, where do you put your party’s odds — and your own — for retaking the White House in 2028?

MARK CARNEY, PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA

You’re in China today, a country with which you’ve opened the door to deeper trade ties. Is this a direct response to Trump’s trade war? Are you optimistic that Canada-U.S. relations can and will improve after the Republicans’ big losses in the U.S. midterm election?

SAM ALTMAN and GREG BROCKMAN, CO-FOUNDERS OF OPENAI

The sell-off of tech stocks has Wall Street on edge. Are you concerned this could sink the valuation of artificial intelligence companies like yours? Voters, too, came out hard against data centers on Election Day. Could this stall the A.I. buildout?

HAILEY BIEBER, FOUNDER AND CHIEF CREATIVE OFFICER OF RHODE AND STRATEGIC ADVISER TO E.L.F. BEAUTY

Can you use social media and celebrity to build an enduring brand, especially in such a competitive sector where consumers’ tastes and trends are notoriously fickle?

SHAYNE COPLAN, C.E.O. OF POLYMARKET; ADENA FRIEDMAN, CHAIR AND C.E.O. OF NASDAQ; and VLAD TENEV, CHAIRMAN AND C.E.O. OF ROBINHOOD

Prediction markets are expected to face increased scrutiny under a Democrat-led Congress. The sector is also facing pressure from state attorneys general. How is that changing your lobbying efforts? For investors, new trading options are emerging all the time, including with tokenized assets and perpetual contracts. In a down market, investors could get burned. Is the industry doing enough to guard against the potential for huge losses?

DAVID ELLISON, CHAIRMAN AND C.E.O. OF SKYDANCE

You’ve taken on $80 billion in debt to build a media giant with brands like CNN and “60 Minutes” that President Trump regularly attacks, or sues. Judging by the share price for Paramount, shareholders aren’t impressed. How do you grow this business in an age of cord-cutting and increasing political pressure?

CHRISTINE LAGARDE, PRESIDENT OF THE EUROPEAN CENTRAL BANK

President Trump has upended trade alliances and ushered in a new era of protectionism. Will this push trading partners away from the U.S.? And since the war with Iran, global bond markets have gone haywire. Are we headed for another debt crisis?

PALMER LUCKEY, A FOUNDER OF ANDURIL INDUSTRIES

Tech companies have become major government defense contractors. Should that flow of taxpayer money be matched with a new era of transparency in the sector, especially as it branches into powerful A.I. weaponry?

ZOHRAN MAMDANI, MAYOR OF NEW YORK CITY

You’ve had a notably warm relationship with President Trump. Can that bond last if he faces increased pressure from Democrats — and from many of the democratic socialists you’ve endorsed? Closer to home, how do you plan to manage your relationship with the business community?

ELON MUSK, FOUNDER AND C.E.O. OF SPACEX AND C.E.O. OF TESLA

You spent roughly $474 million on the U.S. midterm elections, with very little to show for it. Are you done donating to political candidates, or will you double down? Investors are beginning to sour on the A.I. stock trade, and you’ve warned of “guppy-level death” for some. That said, should investors be worried about your companies, too?

SATYA NADELLA, CHAIRMAN AND C.E.O. OF MICROSOFT

You’ve ridden the A.I. boom to become the world’s second most valuable company. But investors are asking tough questions about the future returns on the A.I. build out. Could this be a sign of a bursting A.I. bubble? How confident are you in the economics of A.I. and its ability to withstand a downturn?

We’d like your feedback! Please email thoughts and suggestions to dealbook@nytimes.com.

DealBook, founded 25 years ago by The New York Times columnist Andrew Ross Sorkin, breaks down the most important business news of the day for leaders on Wall Street, in Washington, and beyond.

item.title: Economic and Political Uncertainty Will Be Focus of DealBook Summit
item.description:
This year’s DealBook Summit comes amid heightened uncertainty in corporate America and in Washington, where voter anxiety over economic pressures helped drive a resetting of the political balance of power two weeks ago.

Will the Democrats’ resounding midterm elections victory lead to tougher oversight of businesses, especially Big Tech? Can either party muster the political will to tackle voters’ biggest grievances — namely, the rising cost of living and the rapid spread of data centers in communities across the nation?

Wall Street and Silicon Valley have big concerns, too. Is the latest market sell-off a blip, or a sign that the artificial intelligence rally has run out of steam? Speaking of A.I., will the resignation of Jensen Huang, a founder at Nvidia and the face of the high-flying sector, trigger a drought in deals and investment?

These questions and more will dominate the discussion on Wednesday as Andrew Ross Sorkin, DealBook’s founder, interviews leaders in business, policy and culture.

The morning sessions will feature separate interviews with Christine Lagarde, the European Central Bank’s president, and Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada. Global trade and President Trump’s tariffs will be on the agenda.

U.S. politics will be in focus during interviews with Vice President JD Vance and New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani.

A.I. will be a big theme throughout the day, especially during Mr. Sorkin’s discussion with Sam Altman and Greg Brockman of OpenAI, which is expected to go public some time next year.

Later in the day, Satya Nadella, chief executive of Microsoft, a major investor in OpenAI, will speak on the topic, too.

item.title: Hospitals Rush to Patch Java Vulnerabilities
item.description:
Health networks across the United States rushed to secure computer systems after the discovery of a vulnerability in ubiquitous Java software, searching for signs of intrusion and applying patches that Oracle, Java’s owner, issued as a rapid fix.

The American Hospital Association said it was not aware of any negative impacts on hospital operations, other than the disruption of racing to respond to potential threats with new defenses.

Technology departments were in a race to “patch before they hack,” said John Riggi, the association’s national cybersecurity adviser. Recent system failures including air traffic control, banking and Microsoft software programs, Mr. Riggi said, “have placed hospital cyber teams at an unprecedently high security posture.” The causes of those failures are under review.

“Hospital cybersecurity teams across the country are using sophisticated tools to actively scan their entire internal networks, medical devices and internet-facing programs, searching for instances of the identified Java vulnerability, and patching as soon as possible,” Mr. Riggi said.

The health care industry has been under siege for years by ransomware attacks that have paralyzed their systems while hackers demanded payments of millions of dollars.

Hospital executives rarely disclose whether they paid the ransom, but their settlements in patient class-action lawsuits provide a means of tracking the phenomenon. The health care industry had the highest number of federal court settlements of any sector from 2010 to 2025, with 118, according to a new analysis by Cornerstone Research.

Hospitals use Java in several ways. With its patch on Tuesday, Oracle listed 21 products for which it should be used. Oracle bought Cerner, a large electronic health records vendor, in 2022.

Epic Systems, the largest health records vendor, said Tuesday that its systems were not affected. Judy Faulkner, Epic’s founder and chief executive, disclosed in September that Epic’s own system analysis using artificial intelligence tools had uncovered a flaw that could allow hackers to enter health records systems and possibly change data undetected. It issued a patch.

On Tuesday, consulting and group-purchasing companies for hospitals said that thousands of clients were working around the clock to secure systems. The use of A.I. to examine system integrity and in hacks has dramatically accelerated the pace of cybersecurity response.

“This is the crazy world we live in,” said Florian Quarré, chief data and A.I. officer at Premier, a group purchaser. “This came out hours ago, and is another example of a crack in well- wielded armor that is cracked open with new tools.”

He said the incident had exposed “the complexity related to these flaws in modern systems, the velocity at which they are found and the speed at which they are exploited.”

Security specialists must assume that hackers are using A.I. to exploit flaws in hospital systems, the experts said.

“The key is to move with urgency, follow the evidence as the threat evolves and focus resources where they can meaningfully reduce risk,” said Juli Rhoden Cunningham, chief information security officer at Vizient, a health care consulting company.

Mr. Riggi of the hospital association said that hospital technology teams have been on heightened alert for weeks. Among other cases, he cited a recent hack of the blood storage unit temperature systems in France.

item.title: Google Buys Worker Data From Spirit Airlines in a New Market to Feed A.I.
item.description:
When Spirit Airlines shut down in May, its assets went up for sale: a small fleet of airplanes, coveted slots at LaGuardia Airport and decades of internal workplace data, including employee records, tax forms, 100 million emails and half a billion Microsoft Teams messages.

Google had the winning bid, $10 million, for those employment records, a novel asset class the company said it would use to improve its artificial intelligence products. Imagine what a large language model could glean from the recruiting and timekeeping files of such a large company, or from workers’ snarky chats about their bosses.

But in August, a union representing 5,500 flight attendants affected by the bankruptcy filed an objection in federal court, saying that de-identifying measures promised by Google and Spirit, largely related to the protection of consumer data, were not enough to protect Spirit’s employees.

“If it was not for our union, this would have just happened in a fire sale in the middle of the night,” said Sara Nelson, the president of the Association of Flight Attendants. “This is a brand-new frontier for workers’ rights. It’s making people’s lives, their entire privacy, a commodity.”

Last week, Google agreed to new limitations on the employee data. In a hearing on Tuesday, a bankruptcy judge in federal court in New York State accepted the revised sale terms, and the flight attendants’ union dropped its objections. A spokesman for Google said the company was happy with the result but declined to comment further until the court posted the full language of the agreement.

Data has been sold before in bankruptcies that have raised consumer privacy concerns, like the 2025 bankruptcy of 23andMe, a genetic testing service. And there are examples of a failed company’s records becoming public. After Enron, an energy company, collapsed in 2001, federal investigators released a trove of company emails. They have been mined for case studies and research.

But only recently have companies sought access to a failed company’s internal work force data. There is a market developing, largely out of sight, for the carcasses of dead companies to be turned into feasts for large language models with insatiable appetites for written communication. SpaceX’s A.I. unit has considered buying data from struggling start-ups, Bloomberg reported in September.

The Spirit case appears to be the first large-scale example of using “corporate detritus” to train large language models, said Greg Ewing, a partner at Spencer Fane, a law firm.

“This is a whole new world, where all that data is so valuable to A.I. companies,” Mr. Ewing said. “We are going to see whole marketplaces arise out of it.”

Eric Chafetz, a partner at Lowenstein Sandler, a law firm, said the Spirit case was the first large bankruptcy sale in which a buyer had said it was motivated to build A.I. models. “We have recently received numerous unsolicited inbound inquiries from entities purporting to want to buy similar types of data,” he said. “Parties do believe there’s real value in trying to purchase a failed or failing company’s data.”

This has consequences for employees, Mr. Chafetz said: The bankruptcy code’s privacy protections were designed for consumers. “Employees aren’t in that picture at all,” he said.

Ms. Nelson said personnel files, even if they were cleared of identifying information, could be used to connect private data to a specific employee. A woman’s leave for reproductive care could one day be traced back to her. A pilot’s detailed background check, later uncovered, could expose sensitive personal details.

The flight attendants’ union, which is part of the AFL-CIO, wants to enshrine worker privacy protections into contracts and the law, she said.

“These are standards that can be put into law right away because we already have a major company working on the advancement of these A.I. models, who can comply with these very high standards of protections for workers,” Ms. Nelson said.

The union was joined in its efforts by other unions affected by the Spirit bankruptcy; in all, Ms. Nelson said, about 17,000 workers had been affected by the data privacy issue. In October, more than 120 congressional leaders sent a letter to Google and Spirit asking them to include more protections for employees.

The revised agreement makes clear that certain information is not to be part of the sale, including employee medical and disability records, flight crew fatigue reports and payroll records.

Last week, lawyers for GE Aerospace and CFM International, parts suppliers to Spirit, asked the bankruptcy court to exclude data related to their companies, too, including information related to engine maintenance and avionics systems.

“The data sale poses significant risks to parties that provided such information to the debtors over the years, because Google may use or disclose it through its A.I. products,” they wrote.

item.title: Christine Lagarde on Why She Stepped Down Early From the E.C.B.
item.description:
Christine Lagarde, the president of the European Central Bank, warned on Wednesday that trust was “in short supply” around the world even as it remained fundamental to technology, trade and finance.

“We have to make every effort to secure it, to cherish it and to develop it,” she said in her interview with Andrew Ross Sorkin at the DealBook Summit.

In a wide-ranging conversation, Ms. Lagarde talked about her decision to step down early from her role at the central bank. As president of the bank, which sets interest rates for the 21 countries that use the euro, she has to observe strict political neutrality, something she said she wanted to shed. She’s leaving the role in February, about eight months early and critically ahead of presidential elections next spring in her home country, France.

Ms. Lagarde said she wanted to use her voice and decades of work in international finance against what she said was “fake news” and “misrepresentations” in European elections. “I see it as my duty to clarify, rectify and speak from my position and based on the experience that I’ve had,” she added.

She said that running the World Economic Forum, which hosts the influential annual gathering in Davos, Switzerland, “is one of the options” she is considering to do next. But she didn’t hint at other options, saying she wasn’t going to entertain more speculation while she is still E.C.B. president. “But I’m not retiring,” she added.

Ms. Lagarde also spoke about artificial intelligence and its dominance in the global economy today. It was one reason the European economy has been surprisingly resilient to the fallout of the war in the Middle East, she said. It was also partly why trade has risen in the past couple of years, despite President Trump raising tariffs on many countries.

The companies building A.I. equipment are all over the world, including in Europe. so there is not just a duopoly of dominance between the United States and China, she argued. “We are all in this together,” she said.

But she added that A.I. was highlighting concerns about fairness and the distribution of wealth. She alluded to the Anthropic I.P.O. taking place Thursday, which is set to value the company at more than $1 trillion, making it one of the largest public listings ever. “It raises the question of who is benefiting, how that creation of value will be shared and distributed,” she said.

Ms. Lagarde frequently referred to the ways in which the world is connected and that trust between nations was critical. “International cooperation is a must in this environment where everything moves and affects everybody else,” she said.

item.title: A.I. Bubble Talk Enters the Conversation at DealBook Summit
item.description:
As tech stocks wavered Wednesday morning, conversation at the DealBook Summit turned to bubbles and sky-high valuations for artificial intelligence companies aspiring to go public.

As for the bubble question, opinion differs.

Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank, told Andrew Ross Sorkin in a morning session that she believed there was a “very ambitious price valuation which stands to be corrected eventually.” On the flip side, Sam Altman, chief executive of OpenAI, one of the world’s leading A.I. companies, said there might be “ups and downs of valuations here or there,” but the overall “trend is going to be strong.”

Their comments at the annual summit get at a debate dominating discussion on Wall Street and Silicon Valley, especially with Anthropic expected to price its initial public offering, a possible record-breaker, later on Wednesday. The question on investors’ minds: How fast and how much longer can the A.I. industry keep growing?

Broadly across the industry, investors have become increasingly wary of runaway spending and increasingly lofty valuations of A.I. companies. The Nasdaq Composite index, a benchmark for tech stocks, has tumbled from its October high, underscoring those jitters. In the past month, the beatings have been, in part, driven by the departure of Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, as well as fears of a slowdown in data center build out after Democrats took control of Congress in the midterm elections.
